viewpoint: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been shown to deliver impressive performance in various NLP tasks.

Few-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting includes a few manually crafted step-by-step reasoning demonstrations to enable LLMs to explicitly generate reasoning steps and improve their reasoning task accuracy in multi-step reasoning tasks.
Zero-shot-CoT still suffers from three pitfalls: calculation errors, missing-step errors, and semantic misunderstanding errors.

To address the missing-step errors in multi-step reasoning tasks, we propose the Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting approach, which consists of devising a plan to divide the entire task into smaller subtasks and carrying out the subtasks according to the plan.

To further improve the quality of generated reasoning steps and address calculation errors in multi-step reasoning tasks, we extend the Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting approach with more detailed instructions and derive the PS+ Prompting approach.
Our proposed prompting strategy was evaluated on ten datasets across three reasoning problems.

Our proposed zero-shot prompting, based on Plan-and-Solve and PS+, consistently outperforms Zero-shot-CoT on ten datasets across three reasoning problems by a large margin, is comparable to or exceeds Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought Prompting, and has comparable performance with 8-shot CoT prompting on the math reasoning problem when evaluated over GPT-3.
The code for our proposed approach, Plan-and-Solve Prompting, can be found at the provided GitHub link.
The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in reasoning tasks is heavily influenced by the way they are prompted.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and self-consistency are important methods for improving the ability of LLMs in reasoning tasks.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and self-consistency do not fully utilize the responses generated by LLMs to guide subsequent responses.
The proposed new prompting method, named Progressive-Hint Prompting (PHP), allows for multiple automatic interactions between users and Large Language Models (LLMs).
PHP, the suggested new prompting method, progressively guides toward the correct answers by using previously generated answers as hints.
Progressive-Hint Prompting (PHP) can be easily combined with existing methods like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and self-consistency to enhance performance even more.
The authors carried out extensive and comprehensive experiments using seven benchmarks.
The results reveal that Progressive-Hint Prompting (PHP) boosts accuracy significantly while maintaining efficiency.
With text-davinci-003, Progressive-Hint Prompting (PHP) achieves a 4.2% improvement on GSM8K compared to Complex CoT and a 46.17% reduction in sample paths with self-consistency.
When using GPT-4 and Progressive-Hint Prompting (PHP), state-of-the-art performances are accomplished on SVAMP (89.1% to 91.9%), GSM8K (92% to 95.5%), AQuA (76.4% to 79.9%) and MATH (50.3% to 53.9%).
Large Language Models (LLMs) currently have difficulty with natural language reasoning tasks.
The society of minds concept (Minsky, 1988) motivates the creation of the ReConcile framework, a multi-model multiagent system to enable discussion among diverse LLM agents.
ReConcile improves collaborative reasoning abilities among LLM agents through multiple discussion rounds.
ReConcile teaches LLM agents how to persuade others to better their responses.
ReConcile utilizes a confidence-weighted voting system to arrive at a more accurate consensus.

In each discussion round, ReConcile starts by presenting a 'discussion prompt' with the following components: answers, explanations, and confidence scores from all agents in the previous round, as well as examples of human explanations to help convince other agents.

Experiments on various benchmarks show that ReConcile substantially enhances LLMs' reasoning, surpassing prior single-agent and multi-agent baselines by up to 11.4% and outperforming GPT-4 on three datasets when used individually or as a team.
ReConcile can accommodate various combinations of LLM agents like API-based, open-source, and domain-specific models, resulting in a 8% improvement on the MATH benchmark.
The final analysis shows that the diversity among the individual components of ReConcile is essential for its superior performance.
Code for ReConcile is available at https://github.com/dinobby/ReConcile.
Prompting methods such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) are used to enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models.
Researchers have explored the generation process of rationales and answers with these prompting methods.
Reasoning methods, such as Chain-of-Thought, may be influenced by the quality of the input problems, but this aspect has not been adequately focused on in previous research.
A new method, Self-Polish (SP), is proposed to refine input problems, making them more comprehensible and solvable for large language models.
The Self-Polish method focuses on teaching large language models to eliminate irrelevant information, reorganize logic structures, and group local conditions for better understanding.
The Self-Polish method is compatible with existing prompting methods and can be integrated to enhance their performance.
The Self-Polish method demonstrates strong performance on robustness evaluation.
The question is whether prompting a large language model with explanations improves in-context learning.
The study evaluates the impact of prompting with explanations on two NLP tasks: question answering and natural language inference.
The study compares the performance of four large language models on three textual reasoning datasets using prompts with explanations in multiple styles.

For question answering and natural language inference tasks with prompts that include explanations, small to moderate accuracy improvements are observed over standard few-shot learning for OPT, GPT-3 (davinci), and InstructGPT (text-davinci-001).
For question answering and natural language inference tasks, text-davinci-002 demonstrates more substantial improvements with explanations compared to standard few-shot learning.

The explanations generated by the large language models are found not to necessarily align with the models' predictions or be factually accurate in relation to the input, even in simple tasks with extractive explanations.
Despite the lack of entailment and factual accuracy, flawed explanations can still be used to validate large language models' predictions after the fact.
Explanations deemed good by humans, as they are logically consistent with both the input and the prediction, are more likely to coincide with accurate predictions in the study's three settings.

Based on the inferences from the study, calibrators are trained with automatically acquired scores to evaluate explanation reliability and subsequently enhance performance across all datasets post-hoc.
There is a growing interest in developing next-generation recommender systems based on pretrained large language models.

The semantic gap between natural language and recommendation tasks remains unaddressed, leading to issues such as spuriously-correlated user/item descriptors, ineffective language modeling on user/item contents, and inefficient recommendations via auto-regression.
In this paper, we propose CLLM4Rec, the first generative RS that integrates the LLM paradigm and ID paradigm of RS.
We extend the vocabulary of pretrained LLMs with user/item ID tokens to model the collaborative and content semantics of users and items.
In the pretraining stage, a novel soft+hard prompting strategy is proposed to effectively learn user/item collaborative/content token embeddings via language modeling on RS-specific corpora.

Each document is split into a prompt consisting of heterogeneous soft (user/item) tokens and hard (vocab) tokens and a main text consisting of homogeneous item tokens or vocab tokens, facilitating stable and effective language modeling.
A novel mutual regularization strategy is introduced to encourage the CLLM4Rec to capture recommendation-oriented information from user/item contents.

A novel recommendation-oriented finetuning strategy is proposed for CLLM4Rec, where an item prediction head is added to the pretrained CLLM4Rec to generate recommendations based on the soft+hard prompts established from masked user-item interaction history.
A framework for quantitatively evaluating interactive LLMs is proposed.
An extensive technical evaluation of ChatGPT is conducted using 23 data sets covering 8 different common NLP application tasks.
The multitask, multilingual, and multi-modal aspects of ChatGPT are evaluated using these data sets and a newly designed multimodal dataset.
ChatGPT outperforms LLMs with zero-shot learning on most tasks and, in some cases, outperforms fine-tuned models.
ChatGPT is better at understanding non-Latin script languages than generating them.
ChatGPT is able to generate multimodal content from textual prompts via an intermediate code generation step.
ChatGPT has an average accuracy of 63.41% for reasoning categories, making it an unreliable reasoner.
ChatGPT performs better at deductive reasoning than inductive reasoning.
ChatGPT, like other LLMs, suffers from hallucination problems and generates more extrinsic hallucinations because it does not have access to an external knowledge base.
The interactive feature of ChatGPT allows human collaboration to improve its performance, resulting in an 8% increase in ROUGE-1 on summarization and a 2% increase in ChrF++ on machine translation.
A codebase for evaluation set extraction is released.
ChatGPT's performances on most NLP tasks are still below the performances of supervised baselines.

In this work, we discovered that the subpar performance of ChatGPT on NLP tasks is due to three main factors: (1) the token limit in the prompt does not allow for full utilization of the supervised datasets; (2) a mismatch between the generation nature of ChatGPT and NLP tasks; (3) intrinsic pitfalls of LLMs models, including hallucination and over-focus on certain keywords.
In this work, we propose a collection of general modules to address the issues causing ChatGPT's subpar performance on NLP tasks and improve its performance on these tasks.

Our proposed modules include the following strategies to address the issues causing ChatGPT's subpar performance on NLP tasks: (1) a one-input-multiple-prompts strategy for accommodating more demonstrations; (2) using fine-tuned models for better demonstration retrieval; (3) transforming tasks to formats better suited for the generation nature of ChatGPT; (4) employing reasoning strategies tailored to addressing task-specific complexity; (5) the self-verification strategy to reduce the hallucination issue in LLMs; (6) the paraphrase strategy to improve the robustness of model predictions.

We conduct experiments on 21 datasets, covering 10 representative NLP tasks, including question answering, commonsense reasoning, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, entity-relation extraction, event extraction, dependency parsing, semantic role labeling, and part-of-speech tagging.

Using the proposed combination of techniques, we are able to significantly improve ChatGPT's performance on the selected NLP tasks, achieving performance levels comparable to or better than those of supervised baselines and state-of-the-art models.
Large language models have made progress in natural language processing but their abilities in complex reasoning tasks, like chess, are under-explored.
This paper aims to evaluate the performance of ChatGPT, OpenAI's sophisticated language model, in complex reasoning tasks, using chess as an example.
We evaluate ChatGPT's understanding of the chessboard, compliance with chess rules, and strategic decision-making skills using rigorous metrics analyzing the legality and quality of its moves.
Our evaluation reveals limitations in ChatGPT's attention mechanism that impact its formal language comprehension and exposes the model's underdeveloped self-regulation skills.

Our research shows ChatGPT's tendency to adopt a consistent strategy during gameplay and an increase in decision-making confidence when presented with more natural language or a clearer perception of the chessboard's state.

These findings add to the expanding research on language models beyond natural language processing, offering useful insights for future investigations into models showcasing human-like cognitive capabilities.
